title: Eight Days Out: What This Florida Season Actually Is
author: GatorVault Staff
excerpt: Eight days from FAU, Florida finally has a Week 1 shape — Philo under center, Baugh as the engine, Graham as the heartbeat, and an odd-front defense finding its hybrid language. A season preview for members, not a game plan.
body:
There's a particular quiet that settles over Gainesville in the last week of August — not empty quiet, but the kind that lives between the end of camp and the first real kickoff, when the questions stop being theoretical and start having names. Florida is eight days from Florida Atlantic on a Saturday night in the Swamp, and for the first time since Jon Sumrall walked into the building, the roster has a shape you can hold in your hands.

That shape starts under center. On Aug. 24, Sumrall ended the spring-and-camp suspense the only way a first-year coach can: carefully, with both hands still on the table. Aaron Philo — the Georgia Tech transfer who followed Buster Faulkner south — gets the Week 1 snaps and the lion's share of the ones that matter in practice. Tramell Jones Jr. is not buried. Sumrall said as much out loud, the way coaches do when they mean it, telling Philo this isn't an anointing and telling Jones this isn't a demotion. The separator wasn't arm talent or mobility; Sumrall said those look similar. It was operation: checks, alerts, killing a bad call at the line, seeing the middle of the field. Faulkner's offense is a language, and Philo has been speaking it longer. That is the honest Week 1 board. The season-long truth is that Jones kept closing the gap from April to August, and rooms that stay honest tend to stay dangerous.

If you want the best player on offense, you don't need a committee vote. Jadan Baugh came back, and that decision alone rearranged Florida's ceiling. A thousand-yard rusher in the SEC — 1,170 yards and eight scores a year ago, first-team preseason All-America ink this August, Maxwell and Doak Walker watch lists — he is the back defenses game-plan for and the one Myles Graham still trash-talks in practice like it's personal. Behind him, Evan Pryor, Duke Clark, London Montgomery, and Byron Louis turn "RB1" into a committee without diluting the star. Faulkner's offense wants to be multiple. Baugh makes multiple look like violence.

Around him sits what beat writers have already called, without much hedging, the most talented skill group on either side of the ball. Dallas Wilson, when healthy, is the kind of receiver who resets a first down by existing; Vernell Brown III already led the team as a true freshman and plays with the ball in his hands like he expects the next one. Auburn transfer Eric Singleton Jr. brings senior mileage to the Z; Micah Mays Jr. stole the Orange & Blue and never really gave the spotlight back. The tight end room is newer — Lacota Dippre and Luke Harpring holding the Week 1 leans on our board — and less proven than the receivers, which is fine for September and less fine if the season turns into November and you need a safety valve on third-and-six.

The offensive line walked into camp as the loudest question mark in the building. It walked out of the second scrimmage with Sumrall using the word "jacked." Soft locks for Week 1, per his own presser: Bryce Lovett at left tackle, Knijeah Harris at left guard, Harrison Moore at center, T.J. Shanahan Jr. at right guard, Emeka Ugorji at right tackle. Boyer, Jones, Dice, Kearney — still alive, still in the rotation conversation — which is how you want Year 1 trench depth to sound. Continuity is the ask. Consistency is the sermon Sumrall keeps preaching. Protect Philo, open the cutback for Baugh, and Faulkner's creativity stops being theoretical.

Defense is where the identity might live first. Brad White's odd front is built to be fast and violent — linebacker-friendly, three down linemen eating the double, hybrids free to run to the ball like the whistle is optional. Myles Graham is the best player on that side of the ball — Gainesville kid, 76 tackles a year ago, Butkus watch list, the WILL who treats every meeting like a race he intends to win. Greg Gasparato calls him a leader who goes a hundred miles an hour. Opposite and around him, Jaden Robinson (MIKE) and Aaron Chiles (SAM) give Florida a three-man second level that has already played SEC snaps. Jayden Woods is the JACK — that hybrid edge Sumrall and White love — with KJ Ford and Kofi Asare stacked behind him. Up front, Brendan Bett at nose and Jeramiah McCloud at tackle are the Week 1 leans; LJ McCray leads the end spot.

The secondary is still settling into names, but the hybrid layer already has a face: Kanye Clark holds the STAR lean, the nickel who has to cover the slot and fit the run alley so White's install can stay in base against spread looks. Cormani McClain locks one island; Ben Hanks III leans on the other. Bryce Thornton is the strong safety; DJ Coleman sits ahead at free. White has been blunt about what matters in this league: limit explosives, stay healthy, and have a plan when you don't. JACK and STAR are the report card — Woods and Clark are how that sentence gets said out loud.

Zoom out past the depth chart and you get the season itself. This is not a soft slate. After FAU and Campbell, the road goes through Auburn, then Ole Miss, Missouri, South Carolina, Texas in Austin, Georgia in Atlanta on Halloween, Oklahoma, Kentucky, Vanderbilt, and Florida State. Three recent playoff-caliber programs live on that card. National crystal balls have been living in the 7–5 to 8–4 neighborhood — bowl-eligible, competitive, not yet the finished cathedral Sumrall was hired to build. That feels honest. Four losing seasons in five years leave a bruise; the program talk already frames this year as an attempt to "wake the beast up," with Dave Caldwell in the building and coordinators who've won elsewhere. Culture is the first deliverable. Wins are the proof.

So where do we stand, eight days out? Philo has the keys, not the crown. Baugh is the engine. Graham is the heartbeat. The line has finally given Sumrall a starting five he can say out loud. The receiver room can win you Saturdays if the ball arrives on time. Woods and Clark give the defense its hybrid language. The schedule will not apologize. Year One under Sumrall isn't a coronation and it isn't a rebuild apology note — it's a program choosing a direction in public, with enough talent retained (Baugh, Graham, Woods, Wilson, Brown) to make the direction matter.

September nights in the Swamp have a way of answering questions faster than August pressers. The answers are coming. For now, this is Florida football as it actually sits: clearer than it was in April, tougher than a casual glance at the preseason polls, and finally — after a long stretch of waiting — pointed at something that looks like a season.
takeaways: Philo is Week 1 QB1 (Aug 24) — operation at the line separated him; Jones Jr. stays in the fight.
Baugh is the best offensive player; Graham is the best defender — Year 1 identity starts with both.
OL soft lock Lovett–Harris–Moore–Shanahan–Ugorji walked out of scrimmage two with Sumrall "jacked."
White’s odd front: Woods (JACK) + Clark (STAR) are the hybrid report card; McClain/Hanks, Thornton, Coleman round the back end.
The slate is hard (Texas, Georgia in Atlanta, Ole Miss, Oklahoma). Beat range lives around 7–5 to 8–4 — culture first, wins as proof.

title: Insider: Defensive scheme install ahead of schedule
author: GatorVault Staff
excerpt: Florida's 2026 floor turns on 3-3-5 install pace — JACK/STAR and the trenches — not a laundry list of portal and board stats.
body:
The Big Picture

Florida's 2026 season won't be saved by pedigree on paper. It turns on whether the 3-3-5 hybrid is installed cleanly enough that JACK and STAR can play with leverage by September — not December.

That is the only thesis that matters here: install pace decides whether portal talent becomes SEC snaps or expensive depth-chart clutter.

Inside the Building

JACK/STAR are the report card. Against spread sets, cover-and-rush hybrids win the install; substitution delays lose it. Watch rep winners after the first fall scrimmage more than spring rankings.

Trenches buy time. Three down linemen have to eat doubles so the hybrid layer can play in space. If the front stalls, the scheme looks late no matter how many portal names are on the roster.

Offense must protect the rebuild. Quick-game, play-action, and tempo are not style points — they are survival tools until the OL settles.

What to Watch

First fall scrimmage depth chart at JACK/STAR and DL. If those rooms look settled, the install thesis holds. If they don't, mid-October explosives allowed will tell on Florida long before any bowl talk does.
takeaways: One claim: 3-3-5 install pace — especially JACK/STAR — decides Florida's September floor.
DL must eat doubles or the hybrid layer never gets to play with leverage.
First fall scrimmage is the real report card; spring rankings are noise.
summary: Florida's 2026 floor turns on 3-3-5 install pace — JACK/STAR and the trenches — not a laundry list of portal and board stats.

title: 2026 Portal Class Recap: 23 In, 29 Out
author: GatorVault Staff
excerpt: UF's 2026 transfer cycle in one clean read — who arrived, who left, where exits landed, and which returning defenders anchor the new scheme.
body:
THE HEADLINE — Florida added 23 portal transfers this offseason and confirmed 29 exits. This recap covers the 2026 incoming class only. Prior-cycle enrollees are not counted here.

INCOMING HEADLINERS

  • Eric Singleton Jr. (WR, Auburn) — Immediate WR1 and vertical threat.
  • Aaron Philo (QB, Georgia Tech) — Pro-style distributor in the QB battle.
  • Lacota Dippre (TE) — Starting Y tight end.
  • Five offensive linemen — Harrison Moore (C), Eagan Boyer (LT), TJ Shanahan Jr. (RG), and depth across the front.

RETURNING DEFENSIVE LEADERS — While the portal reshaped the roster, Myles Graham (LB) and Jayden Woods (JACK) return as the communication and edge anchors in {{ coach.DC }}'s 3-3-5. Graham sets the second level; Woods is the scheme's centerpiece off the edge.

PORTAL EXITS — CONFIRMED DESTINATIONS

  • DJ Lagway (QB) — Transferred to Baylor
  • 29 total exits — See Portal Radar for full list with enrolled, committed, and in-portal status

SCHEME FIT GRADE: B+ — The class addressed QB, WR, TE, RB, S, and OL. The biggest question remains cohesion across five new OL starters. Defensive depth behind Graham and Woods is the other watch item.

BOTTOM LINE — On paper, UF fixed every weakness from 2025. Fall camp will decide if the portal class plays to the ceiling or the OL learning curve caps the offense early.
takeaways: 23 incoming transfers — Singleton, Philo, Dippre headline the class
Myles Graham and Jayden Woods anchor the returning defense
29 confirmed exits — DJ Lagway to Baylor among notable departures
OL cohesion is the swing factor for Year 1 under {{ coach.HC }}

title: The 3-3-5 Revolution: Why {{ coach.DC }}'s Scheme Changes Everything
author: GatorVault Film Desk
excerpt: {{ coach.DC }}'s 3-3-5 isn't a gimmick — it's a personnel-driven answer to modern spread offenses. Here's how it works, who benefits, and why Jayden Woods makes it dangerous.
body:
When {{ coach.HC }} hired {{ coach.DC }} from Kentucky, the assumption was UF would run a traditional 4-2-5. Spring camp told a different story. {{ coach.DC }} installed a 3-3-5 hybrid that uses three down linemen to eat double teams, freeing five linebackers and hybrid defenders to flow to the ball.

The front is built around a dominant nose (Brendan Bett) and two versatile ends (LJ McCray, Jeremiah McCloud) who can kick inside on passing downs. The JACK position — occupied by Jayden Woods — is the scheme's centerpiece. Woods sets the edge against the run, drops into coverage on 3rd-and-medium, and rushes the passer on obvious passing downs. He's the reason this defense can stay in base personnel against 11 personnel spread sets.

In the secondary, the STAR/nickel spot is anchored by Kanye Clark, with veteran DJ Coleman rotating in as the second nickel (per post-spring depth charts from GatorCountry and Prep Prospect Report). {{ coach.DC }} wants a defender who can cover slot receivers and fit the run alley. The 3-3-5 lives and dies on assignment discipline — one missed fit creates a 40-yard explosive.

Spring film showed the install ahead of schedule. UF held its own against a talented offense in the spring game, and Woods recorded two TFLs and a strip-sack. The concern: depth behind the starting eleven. If injuries hit the linebacker room, {{ coach.DC }} may need to sub in more traditional 4-man fronts.
takeaways: 3-3-5 uses 3 DL + 3 LB + 5 DB — built for speed and versatility
Jayden Woods at JACK is the scheme's most important piece
STAR: Kanye Clark starts; DJ Coleman is the veteran nickel rotation
Depth is the biggest risk if injuries pile up mid-season

title: {{ coach.HC }}'s First 6 Months: A Real Assessment
author: GatorVault Staff
excerpt: Six months in, {{ coach.HC }} has rebuilt the roster through the portal, installed a new defensive identity, and kept the locker room bought in. We grade every major decision.
body:
{{ coach.HC }} inherited a program in transition. {{ former.Napier }}'s final season left questions at quarterback, offensive line, and defensive scheme. {{ coach.HC }}'s first move was hiring coordinators who fit his culture-first philosophy: {{ coach.DC }} on defense, {{ coach.OC }} on offense, and a revamped S&C staff under {{ staff.SC }}.

The 2026 portal class was the headline. UF added Eric Singleton Jr. (WR), Aaron Philo (QB), Lacota Dippre (TE), Cam Dooley (S), Evan Pryor (RB), and five offensive linemen among 23 incoming transfers. On paper, it addressed every weakness from 2025. Returning defenders Myles Graham (LB) and Jayden Woods (JACK) anchor the second level and edge. The concern: five new OL starters need time to gel, and the QB battle between Tramell Jones Jr. and Philo remains unresolved.

Spring practice was encouraging. The defense looked ahead of schedule — {{ coach.DC }}'s 3-3-5 install clicked faster than expected. The offense showed flashes but struggled with consistency in the red zone. {{ coach.HC }}'s public comments have been measured; he hasn't named a QB starter and has emphasized "earning it in fall camp."

Recruiting remains a top-10 story nationally. The 2027 class sits at No. 8 in the On3 / 247Sports Composite, with Maxwell Hiller as the headliner. {{ coach.HC }}'s staff has maintained relationships from the {{ former.Napier }} era while expanding pipelines in Georgia and Texas.

Our Year 1 projection: 8-4 with a bowl game. The floor is 6-6 if the OL struggles and the QB battle lingers into October. The ceiling is 10-2 if Philo or Jones Jr. takes a leap and the defense stays healthy up front.
takeaways: 2026 portal class addressed QB, WR, TE, S, RB, and OL
Defense is ahead of schedule; offense needs red-zone consistency
QB battle remains unsettled — no public lean heading into fall camp
2027 class No. 8 nationally (On3 / 247Sports Composite), led by Maxwell Hiller
Year 1 projection: 8-4, with 10-2 ceiling if OL and QB click

title: Aaron Philo Film Study: Who Is The New UF Quarterback?
author: GatorVault Film Desk
excerpt: Georgia Tech transfer Aaron Philo brings pro-style mechanics and anticipatory throwing to Gainesville. We broke down 12 games of film to map his strengths, weaknesses, and fit in {{ coach.OC }}'s offense.
body:
Aaron Philo arrived from Georgia Tech as a 6'3", 215-pound quarterback with 47% third-down conversion rate — the best on his GT team in 2025. The film confirms what the stats suggest: Philo is a rhythm passer who thrives when the offense stays on schedule.

Strengths: Philo's best trait is anticipatory throwing. On mesh concepts and levels routes, he throws before the receiver breaks — a skill that translates directly to {{ coach.OC }}'s RPO-heavy system. His arm strength is above average; he drives intermediate crossers with velocity and places back-shoulder throws on the boundary. Mobility is underrated — he's not a runner, but he extends plays with subtle pocket movement.

Weaknesses: Philo can be late on blitz recognition. Against simulated pressure in spring, he held the ball a beat too long on three occasions that would have been sacks in live action. His deep ball accuracy is streaky — when his base is clean, he drops it in; under pressure, he tends to overthrow.

Scheme fit: {{ coach.OC }}'s offense asks the QB to read conflict defenders on RPOs and make quick decisions on play-action. Philo's GT tape shows elite processing on these concepts. The question is whether UF's rebuilt OL can give him a clean enough pocket to operate. If they can, Philo projects as a top-30 QB nationally by Week 8.

Competition note: Tramell Jones Jr. offers more dynamic rushing ability and escapability in the pocket. Philo wins if the offense needs a distributor who limits turnovers. Jones Jr. wins if {{ coach.HC }} wants a dual-threat who can extend drives with his legs.
takeaways: Best trait: anticipatory throwing on mesh and levels concepts
Main concern: blitz recognition and deep-ball consistency under pressure
Fits {{ coach.OC }}'s RPO system if the rebuilt OL protects him
Projects top-30 nationally by Week 8 in best-case scenario

title: War Room: 2026 Schedule Win Probability Model
author: GatorVault Analytics
excerpt: Florida's 2026 model projects ~7.6 expected wins. The season turns on Auburn, Ole Miss, Oklahoma, FSU, and Missouri — with Georgia (Atlanta) and Texas as the stretch games.
body:
GatorVault's 2026 win probability model runs against Florida's full slate: Florida Atlantic, Campbell, Auburn, Ole Miss, Missouri, South Carolina, Texas, Georgia (Atlanta), Oklahoma, Kentucky, Vanderbilt, and Florida State.

Inputs: returning production, portal net value, coaching continuity under {{ coach.HC }}, and site (home / road / neutral). We ran 10,000 simulations per game.

Lock / heavy favorites (85%+): Florida Atlantic (94%), Campbell (96%). These are the only true "should win either way" openers on the slate.

Lean UF (55–75%): Vanderbilt home (72%), South Carolina home (64%), Kentucky away (56%). A night game in Lexington still carries road-SEC variance — unfinished installs get exposed there.

Toss-ups (45–55%): Auburn away (51%), Ole Miss home (50%), Oklahoma home (53%), Florida State away (49%), Missouri away (47%). This five-game cluster decides whether Florida finishes 7-5 or 9-3.

Stretch (under 45%): Georgia in Atlanta (40%), Texas away (37%). Mercedes-Benz Stadium and Austin are the ceiling checks on the calendar.

Expected wins: 7.6. Most likely records: 8-4 (29%), 7-5 (27%), 9-3 (18%). Settled QB play still swings the model by about +1.1 expected wins versus a rotating duo into October.

Bowl projection: ~74% chance of a bowl. An 8-4 finish keeps Orlando / Citrus in play; 9-3 opens a bigger bowl conversation. A late install or unresolved QB race is the fastest path under.500.
takeaways: Expected wins ~7.6; most likely records 8-4 or 7-5.
True toss-ups: Auburn, Ole Miss, Oklahoma, FSU, and Missouri.
Georgia (Atlanta) and Texas (Austin) remain the hardest stretches.
Settled QB play adds about +1.1 expected wins vs. a rotating duo.

title: Summer Camp Preview: 5 Position Battles to Watch
author: GatorVault Staff
excerpt: Fall camp opens August 2nd. These five position battles will shape the starting lineup, the two-deep, and how {{ coach.HC }}'s first season unfolds.
body:
Summer workouts are closed to media, but our sources inside the program point to five battles that will dominate fall camp headlines.

1. Quarterback — Jones Jr. vs. Philo: The biggest story of the offseason. Both quarterbacks have had strong spring moments. Jones Jr. offers dual-threat ability and big-play upside with his legs. Philo brings pro-style poise and third-down efficiency. {{ coach.HC }} has said he won't name a starter until after the FAU game — expect a split in Weeks 1-3.

2. Right Guard — Lovett vs. Shanahan: A genuine dead heat. Both are R-Juniors with starting experience elsewhere. The winner likely starts; the loser becomes the top backup at RG and C.

3. STAR/Nickel — Clark with Coleman rotation: Kanye Clark is the projected starter at STAR (GatorCountry / Prep Prospect Report). DJ Coleman — not Dylan Purter — is the veteran who rotates in as the second nickel while also backing up at FS. Purter and Owens are development pieces behind them.

4. WR (X) — Wilson vs. Mays: Dallas Wilson is projected at X after spring practice reps, though he did not play in the spring game. Micah Mays brings size and veteran savvy and will push in fall camp.

5. OL Right Side — Jones (RT) vs. depth: Caden Jones holds RT, but Eagan Boyer and Javarii Luckas are pushing. If Jones struggles in pass protection against Auburn, Boyer could get a look.

Fall camp report cards drop weekly inside the Vault starting August 5th.
takeaways: QB battle likely splits Weeks 1-3 before a starter emerges
RG (Lovett vs. Shanahan) is a genuine dead heat; STAR is Clark with Coleman rotating in
Wilson projects at WR(X) but did not play in the spring game; Mays is pushing
Weekly fall camp report cards start August 5th in the Vault
